Pip , uv , and Poetry do not currently have a way to verify identity-based attestations described in PEP740. cpanminus does not have a way to verify the integrity of the repository-signed CHECKSUMS file. It once did, but in response to a verification bypass vulnerability , this verification code was removed . Even though PowerShell is supported on non-Windows platforms, Authenticode signature verification is not 9 . At one point, the PowerShell repository noted that this issue “should be fixed in a future release.” Go package management and transparency logs Go’s built-in package manager is the only one I tested that verifies signatures by default, and it also introduces one final concept for cryptographic package integrity. When go get or go mod download fetches a package 10 , it hashes the package contents and compares the hash, package name, and version against the checksum database . The contents of the database are registry-signed (analogous to PGP signatures in Perl’s PAUSE server), and the default checksum database public key is hardcoded in Go’s source code. As long as the checksum database’s private key is used honestly, this design ensures that the package name and version are enough to uniquely identify the binary contents of a package. As a result, the go.mod lockfile achieves package integrity without needing to store cryptographic hashes. 11 Go’s checksum database is an example of a transparency log, or an immutable, global, tamper-resistant log of metadata. The same capability is provided by Sigstore’s Rekor and certificate transparency logs. In package managers, it cryptographically ensures that the package manager only ever installs the same binaries recorded by the transparency log. If everyone agrees on the transparency log, then everyone agrees on the package contents. This makes it more difficult for an adversary to selectively and undetectably target a victim with a malicious package. Transparency logs can still fail if there are other vulnerabilities , the log’s private key is compromised, or no one checks the transparency log for malicious behavior. Of all the package managers I tested, Go performed the best at maintaining cryptographic integrity in the face of a compromised package repository or proxy. However, the registry-signature-like design means that much of the system’s trust is concentrated in a single private key. A proposed cryptographic design for package managers One potential approach that combines the ideas in this post is to include signature information in the lockfile. Rather than commit to the hash of a particular package, the lockfile could commit to a developer’s identity or public key. This reuses much of the infrastructure in place for lockfile hashes, but it separates the question of immediate updates from the question of package integrity. With this design, the lockfile could specify a single dependency version (for build reproducibility) or a lower bound (for immediate updates), and the included identity ensures that a malicious repository or proxy cannot easily tamper with whatever package version the manager resolves to. In addition, a transparency log can protect against selective targeting, building on Sigstore’s identity-based signing and transparency log service. Sigstore avoids long-lived keys by default, but it also supports self-managed keys, KMS providers, and hardware tokens. This gives an easily adopted and secure default while still giving flexibility to developers who desire more control over their keys. This idea is not new and not my own. Attestation identities are part of the pylock.toml Python lockfile specification , the trusted-keys in Gradle’s verification metadata , and the pgp-keys-map.list file in the pgpverify-maven-plugin for Maven. This is the direction that many package managers are already moving towards, as evidenced by the increasing adoption of Sigstore into publishing workflows, attention on supply-chain security, and bugfixes that specifically cite potential tampering by a malicious adversary. There is increasing recognition that this is a problem, and increasing appetite to fix it. It won’t be easy. There are many subtle nuances that have to be considered and addressed, signing verification code needs to be developed and audited, and developers need to adopt the resulting design. In many of the package managers I reviewed as part of this project, I found communities of people who have been thinking about and pushing for cryptographic integrity and package signing for years. They know best what those package managers need, and they deserve the resources to make this a reality. One of the greatest cryptographic success stories in the past decade has been the nearly universal adoption of HTTPS, driven in part by industry and community recognition of the security risks of unencrypted traffic, and the nonprofit Let’s Encrypt providing free and easy-to-use TLS certificates as a public good. Package signing is in a similar state now to where HTTPS was a decade ago: persistent adversaries are a huge concern, and cryptographic security is nearly nonexistent. Universal package signing is not here yet, but it is on the horizon. With the right attention and investment, we can make it a reality. For consistency with other package managers, we do not consider this question, and we note this as a limitation of our threat model. ↩︎ Gradle can have a verification-metadata.xml file with content hashes, even though gradle.lockfile does not. ↩︎ Note that some flutter subcommands, including flutter run and flutter test , call flutter pub get by default, so these commands can also overwrite the pubspec.lock file unless called with --no-pub . ↩︎ The SwiftPM client has two main ways to download packages: via Git and via the custom Swift Package Registry Service Specification. items.headline: Hidden Curves and Short Duals: Cubic Jets, Dual Leaks, and the Limits of Masked-Code Encryption
items.summary: Masked-code encryption hides a decodable code behind a transformation meant to make it look random. We study the two masks proposed as compact alternatives to Goppa codes---Wang's RLCE and the $(U\,|\,U{+}V)$ construction of UVW-KEM---over the decodable hidden codes they have been or could be applied to, and find that, among the families examined, none yields a compact trapdoor. Over Reed--Solomon and algebraic-geometry codes the mask hides a \emph{curve}, and curves are not hidden from jets.

Every proposed UVW parameter set has the predicted cubic deficiency (key recovery has been demonstrated at UVW-KEM-128). RLCE's long-key regime $w\ge n-k$, out of reach of the square-code attack for eight years, falls at degree three: on a full-size Level-1 parameter set we recover an equivalent key from the public key alone and decrypt fresh ciphertexts. HermitianRLCE is distinguished the same way. A forcing law, a master count and a redundancy law make the \emph{jet degree} an invariant of hidden-pairing codes: within that model, each unit of structural depth costs a unit of redundancy. items.headline: Provenance Proofs: Linkable Zero-Knowledge Derivation Relations for Hierarchical Deterministic Wallets
items.summary: ZKPoSP proves that a public key or address was honestly derived from a hidden wallet seed, without revealing the seed or the private derivation state. This paper studies relationships among several derived values: whether public keys or addresses, possibly on different curves and different blockchains, share a hidden origin, which is the seed or an anchor of the wallet, and who else can recognize this relation. We give a model for such provenance proofs, with derivation proofs, which carry a link value, and provenance proofs, which show that several derivation statements share an origin.

items.headline: (R)Icy-DVRF: A Robust Distributed Verifiable Random Function Based on ROAST Signatures
items.summary: Ensuring robustness and liveness in distributed verifiable random functions (DVRFs) allows the protocol to maintain correct operation and guarantee output generation, even in the presence of malicious actors attempting to disrupt the process, delay cryptographic shares, or remain unresponsive. Because existing DVRF protocols typically rely on synchronous or semi-synchronous network assumptions, simultaneously achieving these properties remains a challenge. To address this limitation, this paper enhances the FROST-based Icy-DVRF protocol to achieve both robustness and liveness.

items.headline: A proof of P≠NP (New symmetric encryption algorithm against any linear attacks and differential attacks)
items.summary: P vs NP problem is the most important unresolved problem in the field of computational complexity. Its impact has penetrated into all aspects of algorithm design, especially in the field of cryptography. The security of cryptographic algorithms based on short keys depends on whether P is equal to NP.

detail.findings_tradeoffs: In fact, the security requirements for cryptographic keys are much stricter than those for P$\neq$NP, the security of the key must ensure not only a sufficiently high computational complexity to crack it, but also consider the security of each bit of the key, while fully avoiding the effectiveness of various attack methods. In this paper, we innovatively propose a new encoding mechanism and develop a novel block symmetric encryption algorithm, which be named Eagle, whose encryption and decryption can be completed in linear time. The key consists of 12 variables, for the attacker, in the case when only the plaintext-ciphertext correspondence is known, the problem of cracking the key is equivalent to solving a system of equations about 12 unknown variables $(w_{1}, w_{2}, ..., w_{11}, w_{12})$ together with some implicit variables which are generated by the encryption process. In this paper, we will prove that there is no universal algorithm without brute-force searching at least one variable during the process of verifying five variables $(w_{1}$, $w_{2}$, $w_{3}$, $w_{4}$, $w_{9})$ whose computational complexity is not greater than solving the 12 variables. After performing elimination the implicit variables, the problem of verifying the five variables will be equivalently transformed into a series of general quintic equations about one variable $w_{11} \oplus w_{12}$ with coefficient given by other six variables $(w_{5}$, $w_{6}$, $w_{7}$, $w_{8}$, $w_{10}$, $w_{11})$, according to the conclusion that ``there is no algebraic solution to quintic equations", we can't establish a system of algebraic equations only containing the six variables $(w_{5}$, $w_{6}$, $w_{7}$, $w_{8}$, $w_{10}$, $w_{11})$ without $w_{11} \oplus w_{12}$. Without solving the six variables, the problem of verifying the five variables $(w_{1}$, $w_{2}$, $w_{3}$, $w_{4}$, $w_{9})$ is equivalent to solve the slope of a line given only the x-coordinates of several points on it, this implies that there is no universal algorithm without brute-force searching at least one variable to verify the five variables $(w_{1}$, $w_{2}$, $w_{3}$, $w_{4}$, $w_{9})$. Since the computational complexity of brute-force searching any single variable is exponential, thus the complexity of cracking the key is exponential. Thus decryption is a one-way function, and according to ``the existence of one-way function means P$\neq$NP", solving the unsolved problem of P vs NP. In addition, we further constructed another block symmetric encryption algorithm, which be named $Eagle^{*}$. The key of $Eagle^{*}$ is composed of three independent variables. Given any plaintext ciphertext correspondences, the problem of verifying any two variables in the key is equivalent to solving a system of quintic equations. Based on the conclusion that there is no algebraic solution to quintic equations, we assert that there is no fast algorithm to verify any two variables, and thus the computational complexity of cracking the key is equal to the computational complexity of completely exhausting the three variables. In addition, we conducted an in-depth analysis that without cracking the key, it is not possible to directly decrypt new ciphertext by simply collecting a large number of ciphertext plaintext correspondences. Due to the fact that ciphertext consists of four parts, three parts are completely random, while the other small part is calculated using plaintexts, keys, and random numbers, and their distribution is also completely random, thus $Eagle^{*}$ is resistant to all forms of linear and differential attacks.

It is an open question whether $ρ_n$ tends to~1 as $n$ grows. We show that with agent redundancy, the answer to this question is positive. That is, for every $ε> 0$, $ρ_{ε, n}$ tends to~1 as $n$ grows. Adapting our techniques to a related setting, we also improve a recent result of Ezra and Garbuz, and show that without agent redundancy, there always exists an allocation that gives $n - O(\log^2 n)$ agents their full MMS.

items.headline: Tight Analysis of Randomized Truthful Scheduling: An $(m+1)/2$ Lower Bound
items.summary: The Nisan-Ronen conjecture, a central problem in algorithmic game theory, asserts that no deterministic truthful mechanism for makespan minimization on $m$ unrelated machines can achieve an approximation ratio better than $m$. Christodoulou, Koutsoupias, and Kovács resolved it in 2023, but the optimal approximation ratio achievable by randomized truthful mechanisms remained open. Recently, Anastasiadis, Christodoulou, Koutsoupias, Kovács, and Schecker extended techniques from the deterministic proof to establish a $(3/2-\sqrt{2})(m-1)$ lower bound for universally truthful mechanisms with discrete support and gave a universally truthful mechanism with approximation ratio $m/2+o(m)$.

We prove that the optimal approximation ratio is $(n+1)/2$ for every $n\ge7$, relative to the minimum makespan of an integral assignment. The lower bound holds for every $n$ and allows unrestricted computation and arbitrary correlations among assignments, assuming finite expected payments and a guarantee uniform over all finite job counts. The matching mechanism uses correlated rounding and runs in expected polynomial bit time on rational inputs. These guarantees hold for all finite nonnegative processing times. items.headline: Modelling lock-in of AI adoption through skill erosion. Generative AI can improve immediate performance but may erode the human skills required for future work.
items.summary: Generative AI can improve immediate performance but may erode the human skills required for future work. We study a model in which individuals tend to imitate successful peers, while their independent skills grow with practice and erode with reliance on AI. Because each agent's skill reflects their history, non-users and AI users develop different skill distributions, which we derive exactly.

detail.findings_tradeoffs: Skill erosion can produce bistability and hysteresis between a low-adoption, high-skill state and a high-adoption, low-skill state. When agents rarely change behaviour at random, the two transitions are asymmetric. A single AI user spreads through a population of experts only if AI-assisted work earns more than expert work, whatever the timescale of skill adaptation. A single non-user, by contrast, can lead an AI-dependent population back to independent work only if they regain enough skill before returning to AI, which becomes easier the more persistent behaviours are. As AI improves, adoption can jump abruptly, and a sufficiently long increase in its benefit, such as a period of low prices, can leave a population relying on AI after the benefit has returned to its initial value. Skill erosion thus creates a history-dependent switching cost that can make widespread AI adoption difficult to reverse.

items.summary: We study randomized allocations (lotteries) of indivisible chores under additive costs and introduce the notion of MMS1, which requires each agent's bundle to satisfy the maximin share (MMS) bound after the removal of at most one chore. Our main result establishes that every instance admits an ex-ante proportional lottery in whose support every allocation is MMS1 and all but $o(n)$ agents satisfy MMS. Consequently, every realized allocation can be made MMS by disposing of at most $o(n)$ chores.
